concept.name: Rising wedge
concept.definition: A technical-analysis pattern in which price makes higher highs and higher lows but both bounding trend lines slope upward and converge, compressing the advance. When it appears in an uptrend it is read as a bearish reversal warning (momentum fading into the apex); in a downtrend it is read as a bearish continuation (a corrective rally). It is an analytical hypothesis, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: Price is still rising, but each push up is smaller than the last — buyers are paying more for less progress, and the advance typically resolves downward through the lower line.
concept.mechanics: Draw two upward-sloping, converging trend lines connecting at least two (preferably three) highs and lows; volume usually declines as the wedge forms. The signal is a break of the lower trend line; traders may enter short on the break with a stop above the wedge. Unlike the symmetrical triangle, both lines slope in the same direction, which is what gives the wedge its directional bias.
concept.failure_modes: In strong bull trends a rising wedge can keep grinding higher far longer than expected, producing repeated premature short entries; the 'breakdown' can also be a brief shakeout followed by an upside resolution. Convergence is subjective — different trend-line anchors produce different 'wedges' on the same chart.
concept.misconceptions: That a rising wedge must always break down — it is a tendency, and the same shape in a downtrend is a continuation pattern whose 'signal' only activates on the lower-line break. It is also often confused with an ascending triangle, whose top line is horizontal rather than rising.
concept.example: A stock climbs from $40 to $55 over two months with each successive high only marginally above the last and volume shrinking; a close below the rising lower trend line at $52 triggers the bearish reading.
